The subject pursues a qaḏiye; the enumeration profiles what he gives up in doing so. Direct themes share possessive reference to the agent, but that does not make the verb Detransitive. No literal ritual, death, willingness or technical sense can be isolated from this one modern prose example. The k-prefixed Infectum describes a general pattern; it does not establish a new box.
Kəmḏaḥe is copied with the source’s plain ḏ, not silently changed to the root’s ḏ̣. The apparent spelling difference and literary resource list are evidence to check, not grounds for a new stem.
Is b-nafš- obligatory for self-sacrifice with this verb, and how does added d ruḥe affect emphasis? A single coreferential example cannot establish a full argument paradigm.
Can speakers use ḏ̣ḥy for literal ritual sacrifice or ordinary costly volunteering outside this remedy quest? No broader numbered sense is added without contrastive evidence.
